items.name: Guardian Journal
items.description: Your field diary. Open it with J to revisit a choice, finish a note or follow a source.

items.name: Date-Kind Lens
items.description: A concept tool. It shows WHAT a date describes: a grant, a build, a catalogue range or a claim. It cannot tell you if the date is correct.

items.name: Field Annotation Pen
items.description: Adds lasting notes to your records. It never changes the dates in a source document.

items.name: Provenance Thread
items.description: A concept tool. It follows an object from hand to hand and marks where the record stops. It cannot show what nobody wrote down.

items.name: Small gold seal
items.description: Pressed into the back of Corvan's old sign. A ring with a mark that nobody here recognises.

items.name: Emberford town map
items.description: A free hand-drawn map of the market, the forge and the guild hall.

items.name: Ember tea
items.description: A lidded cup from Emberford market. It keeps its heat on the walk. There is room for two on the bench by the supper hatch.

misconceptions.title: Science gives final certainty
misconceptions.signal: Labels a measured claim as exact or proven, with no range.
misconceptions.worldResponse: Visitors ask: 'Exact for how long?' A later record gives a different number.
misconceptions.reflection: Which part of the claim is measured, and how big could the error be? What would make you change the number?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Ask for a range with every measured claim. Compare an early estimate with a later one.

misconceptions.title: All views have equal support
misconceptions.signal: Treats a claim with evidence and a claim without evidence as equally strong.
misconceptions.worldResponse: The crowd follows the weaker claim, and it gives way.
misconceptions.reflection: Two people can both have a view. Do both views have the same support? What would you check?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Separate 'everyone has a perspective' from 'every claim has the same evidence'.

misconceptions.title: Having a position means being biased
misconceptions.signal: Throws out a source only because the person has a position.
misconceptions.worldResponse: With every 'biased' source gone, nobody is left who knows how the thing was made.
misconceptions.reflection: Everyone who knows something knows it from somewhere. What does this person's position let them see?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Separate 'this person has a position' from 'this claim is badly supported'. Ask what the position adds.

misconceptions.title: Objective means having no point of view
misconceptions.signal: Asks for a source with no point of view at all.
misconceptions.worldResponse: The archive has no such source. Every record was made by someone, for some reason.
misconceptions.reflection: If no source is from nowhere, what makes a source more or less trustworthy?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Present objectivity as a method: checking, comparing and being open to correction.

misconceptions.title: More sources always mean a stronger claim
misconceptions.signal: Counts how many people repeat a claim, without asking if they share one origin.
misconceptions.worldResponse: The Provenance Thread shows that several reports go back to one origin.
misconceptions.reflection: Three people told you. How many of them saw it themselves?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Independence of sources: count origins, not copies.

misconceptions.title: If it is displayed, it is true
misconceptions.signal: Accepts a printed or displayed label without checking it.
misconceptions.worldResponse: A museum label or crate label turns out to be a copying mistake.
misconceptions.reflection: Who wrote this label, and what did they check?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Provenance and authority of displays.

misconceptions.title: Things that happen together must be cause and effect
misconceptions.signal: Names a cause because two things happen together.
misconceptions.worldResponse: A third thing turns up that explains both.
misconceptions.reflection: What else changed at the same time? How could you test one cause on its own?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Use a simple example with a hidden third factor. Ask the class how to control for it.

misconceptions.title: One case proves a rule
misconceptions.signal: Makes a general claim from one vivid case.
misconceptions.worldResponse: The next case is different.
misconceptions.reflection: How many cases have you seen? What would a different case look like?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Sampling and how far one case can reach.

misconceptions.title: Old knowledge is wrong knowledge
misconceptions.signal: Dismisses a record because it is old.
misconceptions.worldResponse: An old record turns out to be accurate for what it records.
misconceptions.reflection: Is the record wrong, or is it about a different question?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Date a claim; ask what was known and recorded at the time.

misconceptions.title: Art cannot tell us anything
misconceptions.signal: Dismisses a song or artwork as 'just art' when it carries information.
misconceptions.worldResponse: The song holds a detail that the written records missed.
misconceptions.reflection: What can a song, picture or pattern hold that a list of facts cannot?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Pair an artwork with a document about the same thing. Ask what each one shows.

misconceptions.title: Mathematics is only facts, with no assumptions
misconceptions.signal: Treats a calculated result as certain without asking what went into it.
misconceptions.worldResponse: A result changes when a measurement or an assumption behind it changes.
misconceptions.reflection: What measurements and assumptions went into this number? Which one, if changed, would change the result?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Show one calculation with two different starting assumptions.

misconceptions.title: Mathematics has nothing to do with culture
misconceptions.signal: Says that where a method came from does not matter.
misconceptions.worldResponse: The units, tools and purposes behind a method turn out to shape the result.
misconceptions.reflection: Who used this method, with what units and tools, and for what purpose?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Trace one method across places and centuries. Ask what changed on the way.

misconceptions.title: A record shows exactly what happened
misconceptions.signal: Treats a ledger or chronicle as a direct copy of the past.
misconceptions.worldResponse: A second record of the same event says something different.
misconceptions.reflection: Who wrote this record, for what purpose, and what did they leave out?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Compare two records of one event. Ask why they differ.

misconceptions.title: The official account is the only account
misconceptions.signal: Uses only the official or ruling source and ignores others.
misconceptions.worldResponse: An older or quieter voice adds a part of the story that the official record leaves out.
misconceptions.reflection: Whose account is this? Whose account is missing, and where could you find it?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Look for the voices that official records leave out. Ask how we can recover them.

misconceptions.title: Asking people is not real evidence
misconceptions.signal: Dismisses what people report as mere gossip, with no thought of method.
misconceptions.worldResponse: A careful set of reports, checked against each other, answers the question.
misconceptions.reflection: How could you ask many people in a way that you can check?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Compare gossip with a careful survey. Ask what makes the second one evidence.

misconceptions.title: Experts are right about everything
misconceptions.signal: Accepts an expert's view on a question outside their field.
misconceptions.worldResponse: The expert points out the limit of their own field.
misconceptions.reflection: What is this person expert in? Is this question inside it?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Scope of expertise.

misconceptions.title: Experts cannot be trusted at all
misconceptions.signal: Rejects all experts because one expert made a mistake.
misconceptions.worldResponse: Without any expert advice, a simple problem becomes hard to solve.
misconceptions.reflection: When is it sensible to trust an expert? What would make you trust one more, or less?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Discuss calibrated trust: trust in a field, for what can be checked, and how errors are corrected.

misconceptions.title: My own experience is the best evidence
misconceptions.signal: Accepts only what they saw for themselves.
misconceptions.worldResponse: A second observer noticed something the player could not see.
misconceptions.reflection: What could another observer notice that you missed? How can you check your own seeing?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Compare two eye-witness accounts. Discuss the limits of perception and memory.

misconceptions.title: A translation says exactly what the original says
misconceptions.signal: Treats a translated word as the same as the original.
misconceptions.worldResponse: Two translations of the same word make two different claims.
misconceptions.reflection: What does the word claim in each language? What could be lost or added?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Take one key word in two translations. Ask what each choice claims.

misconceptions.title: Names are only labels and change nothing
misconceptions.signal: Says a name does not matter when it carries a claim or a history.
misconceptions.worldResponse: A name turns out to hold a story about who had the right to name the place.
misconceptions.reflection: What does this name claim? Who gave it, and what other names are there?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Compare a local name with an official name for the same place. Ask what each one tells.

misconceptions.title: Tools are neutral
misconceptions.signal: Says that a tool has no effect on what we can make or know.
misconceptions.worldResponse: The tool turns out to decide what can be made, and what can be seen.
misconceptions.reflection: What does this tool make easy? What does it make hard, or impossible?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Ask what one instrument or tool lets people notice, and what it hides.

misconceptions.title: Machines cannot be wrong
misconceptions.signal: Trusts a machine's output over a check.
misconceptions.worldResponse: The machine's source turns out not to exist.
misconceptions.reflection: How would you check what a machine gives you? What would count as a check?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Show a machine output with an invented source. Practise checking it.

misconceptions.title: Religion and science must always conflict
misconceptions.signal: Dismisses a scholar's work on nature because the scholar was religious.
misconceptions.worldResponse: Many scholars worked on faith and on nature, and asked different questions of each.
misconceptions.reflection: What question does each part of this person's work try to answer?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Discuss scope: different questions, different methods. Use figures who worked in both.

misconceptions.title: Ethics is only feeling, with no reasons
misconceptions.signal: Refuses to give or hear reasons in a disagreement about values.
misconceptions.worldResponse: Without reasons, the people cannot reach any agreement.
misconceptions.reflection: You may still disagree. What reasons could each side give?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Ask for reasons on both sides of one value disagreement. Do not ask for a winner.

misconceptions.title: Only writing counts as knowledge
misconceptions.signal: Ignores an oral source because it is not written.
misconceptions.worldResponse: The spoken tradition agrees with the physical evidence where the written record is silent.
misconceptions.reflection: How is a spoken tradition kept accurate? How could you check it against other evidence?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Show a case where an oral tradition and other evidence agree. Discuss how oral knowledge is kept.

misconceptions.title: A famous person did it alone
misconceptions.signal: Credits one person for work that a team did.
misconceptions.worldResponse: Visitors retell the story and the other people drop out of it.
misconceptions.reflection: Who else is named in your cards? Why might they be forgotten?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Collective knowledge and hidden hands.

misconceptions.title: 'First' means the first person with the idea
misconceptions.signal: Uses 'first' with no criterion: first at what?
misconceptions.worldResponse: Patent, practical pen and object dates disagree, and the label glows.
misconceptions.reflection: First at what? A patent, a working thing, a sale, a record?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Defining 'first' with a criterion and a limit.

misconceptions.title: A theory is just a guess
misconceptions.signal: Calls a tested explanation 'only a theory' as if that meant a guess.
misconceptions.worldResponse: The explanation predicts what happens next, and it does.
misconceptions.reflection: What has this explanation predicted? What would show it is wrong?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Separate everyday 'theory' (a hunch) from a tested explanation.

misconceptions.title: A model is a copy of reality
misconceptions.signal: Treats a model or reconstruction as the real thing.
misconceptions.worldResponse: Visitors take a modern model for a historical object.
misconceptions.reflection: What does the model show, and what was added when it was made?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Purpose and limits of models.

misconceptions.title: A myth or song is just a false story
misconceptions.signal: Calls a traditional story false and stops there.
misconceptions.worldResponse: The story turns out to carry real knowledge: a name, a place, a value.
misconceptions.reflection: What does this story explain or keep? What would you check it against?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Ask what a myth or song does for the people who keep it, not only whether it is literally true.

misconceptions.title: Numbers speak for themselves
misconceptions.signal: Presents a number with no choice about what it measures or shows.
misconceptions.worldResponse: The same number, framed two ways, makes visitors believe two different things.
misconceptions.reflection: Which question does this number answer? What did someone choose when they showed it?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Show one data set in two framings. Ask the class which choices changed the message.

misconceptions.title: Being sure means being right
misconceptions.signal: Makes a very strong claim on weak support.
misconceptions.worldResponse: The over-confident claim cracks in the Showdown, and the Fray grows on it.
misconceptions.reflection: How strong is your support? Would a smaller claim hold better?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Confidence calibration: match force to support.

misconceptions.title: An essay only needs to describe
misconceptions.signal: Wants to describe sources instead of making an argument.
misconceptions.worldResponse: The reader asks 'so what?' and walks away.
misconceptions.reflection: What is your claim? What would someone who disagrees say?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Turn a description into a claim, then add a counterclaim.

misconceptions.title: Admitting a fair point makes you weaker
misconceptions.signal: Answers a fair point with a shout or a cheap shot instead of dealing with it.
misconceptions.worldResponse: The crowd notices the dodge and trusts the player less.
misconceptions.reflection: What would happen to your argument if you accepted the fair point and then answered it?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Show how a counterclaim, answered well, makes an argument stronger.

misconceptions.title: Only impressive objects are worth showing
misconceptions.signal: Ignores a small or plain object because it is not grand.
misconceptions.worldResponse: The small object turns out to hold the important clue.
misconceptions.reflection: What can a small, plain object show that a grand one cannot?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Choose a plain personal object and ask what it shows about knowledge.

misconceptions.title: A knowledge question is the same as a subject question
misconceptions.signal: Answers with subject content when the question is about how we know.
misconceptions.worldResponse: The answer gives a fact, but the disagreement goes on.
misconceptions.reflection: Is your question about the pen, or about how we decide what counts as 'first'?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Take one subject question and turn it into a question about knowledge.

misconceptions.title: Real examples must come from the news
misconceptions.signal: Wants only today's events as real examples.
misconceptions.worldResponse: A dated historical object or a personal experience works just as well.
misconceptions.reflection: Which real examples can you check carefully? Do they have to be recent?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Collect examples from history, from the student's own life and from subjects.

misconceptions.title: If we are not sure, we know nothing
misconceptions.signal: Gives up when the evidence is partial.
misconceptions.worldResponse: A partial clue is still enough to act on, with care.
misconceptions.reflection: What do you know, even if you are not sure of everything? What could you do with that?
misconceptions.teacherMove: Use a range or a 'probably' to show how partial knowledge still guides action.
